newsitem.title: THAILAND: Foreign ownership plan no cure for Thai property.
newsitem.headline: Foreign ownership plan no cure for Thai property.

text.p: A Thai plan to let foreigners own condominiums is the latest move to help the country's ailing property sector but analysts said on Wednesday it still fails to solve the fundamental problems of oversupply and high prices.

"This is not the saviour for the market," said one analyst, referring to the Thai cabinet's decision on Tuesday to allow an increase in foreign ownership of condominiums to 100 percent from 40 percent.
Thailand's property sector is now paying the price for rapid, haphazard expansion during the country's boom years, analysts said.

The sector has been grappling with a host of problems such as a major supply glut, double-digit interest rates which have further sapped lacklustre demand, and over-leveraged, inexperienced property and development companies which have begun to collapse.
At the same time, the economy is slowing with annual growth in gross domestic product seen slipping to around an 11-year low of between five and six percent this year.
Over the past months the government has approved a number of measures to bolster the sector, ranging from a large bond issue to mortgage fee cuts and tax exemptions for home buyers.
Thailand hopes the latest move to ease foreign ownership laws will bring some needed investment into the market.
But most analysts were sceptical, adding that there was not enough foreign demand to fill the current 40 percent foreign ownership limit.

"Some demand will come through, but foreigners will research it pretty well in terms of supply and demand," an analyst said. "They will realise that pricing is the thing that is out of whack at the moment."
Industry experts say the residential housing sector in Bangkok is hugely over-supplied, with 300,000 to 400,000 vacant housing units -- about half of which are condominiums.
At current demand levels it will take at least three years to absorb all the supply, they said.

"In the luxury condominium sector, in the downtown Bangkok area, the occupancy level is 57.6 percent and it will decrease to about 50 percent by the end of the year because there's still a lot of new supply coming on," said Philip Finch, research manager at property firm Richard Ellis.
He said the new law was not expected to help individual buyers much, mainly because there is no mechanism to help finance residential purchases by foreigners.

"Right now, foreigners can't borrow money from Thai banks to buy property, and foreign banks won't lend it to them either," Finch said. "They have to have cash up front, so it's very, very difficult."
Foreign institutional investors interested in buying entire condominium complexes are the most likely group to benefit from the new law, the analysts said.
Dozens of potential investors have been looking at the sector recently, they said. But few have actually bought.
"At the end of the day it will be dependent on price reduction," said Finch.

"It's more appealing for overseas institutional investors, but they want double digit yields and to get that they need a 15 to 20 percent decrease in prices," he said, noting yields are now about seven to eight percent.
He and other analysts said most of the measures approved by the government have been geared toward artificially supporting prices and pushing demand up to meet the prices.
"When there is oversupply the prices come down to meet demand, but this isn't happening here," said one analyst. "The market here isn't allowed to work properly."
